407.title: Solomon asks (1 Kings 3)
407.hook: offered anything, a young king asks for an understanding heart
407.howItsDone: Catholics read the Book of Wisdom, one of the deuterocanonical books, in the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours, and count wisdom first among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit received in confirmation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David weeping above the gate: my son Absalom. Your line was would god I had died for thee. Who in your family did you reach toward? Day four hundred seven, and a new week.
screen: `WOULD GOD I HAD DIED FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: If God appeared to you tonight in a dream and said, ask whatever you want, what would you ask for? Be honest. Money that would end the worrying. A long, healthy life. Somebody's mind changed. It happens to a young man named Solomon, David's son, newly king. He has gone to the high place at Gibeon to offer sacrifice, and that night the Lord appears to him in a dream and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Ask what thou wilt that I should give thee." No limits. Solomon's answer is today's word.
screen: `ASK FOR ANYTHING.` → `A NEW KING AT GIBEON.` → `ASK WHAT THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: Solomon starts with honesty. "I am but a child, and know not how to go out and come in." He's king of a huge people and he doesn't know how to begin. So he asks: "Give therefore to thy servant an understanding heart, to judge thy people, and discern between good and evil." In Hebrew it's even more striking. Solomon asks for a lev shomea, a listening heart. The same word as the boy Samuel's thy servant heareth. Wisdom, in this story, starts with listening. And God is pleased. Because you didn't ask for long life, or riches, or your enemies' lives, he says, I give you a wise and understanding heart, and the things you didn't ask for too. Then, right away, the chapter shows what that heart looks like. Two women come before the king, sharing one house, each with a newborn. One baby died in the night. Both claim the living child. No witnesses. Solomon calls for a sword: divide the living child in two. One woman says, fine, divide it. The other cries out: give her the child, just don't kill him. And Solomon knows the mother: the one who would rather lose her son than see him die. That's wisdom here: not cleverness, but seeing into a heart. The Catholic Bible keeps a whole book in Solomon's voice, the Book of Wisdom, one of the seven books Catholics count in the Old Testament that many Protestant Bibles leave out or set apart. In it, the speaker remembers this moment: "I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came upon me." And the Church counts wisdom first among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.
screen: `I AM BUT A CHILD.` · `A LISTENING HEART.` · `TWO MOTHERS AND A SWORD.` · `THE BOOK OF WISDOM.` · then, large: `GIVE THY SERVANT AN UNDERSTANDING HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for wisdom today. Settle, and breathe. Think of one decision on your plate where you honestly don't know how to go out and come in. A conversation you dread. A choice at work. Something with your kids or your parents. Now, instead of asking for the outcome you want, ask for a listening heart about it. If you pray, you can use Solomon's words: give thy servant an understanding heart. Then listen. To the people involved, to your own conscience, to the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Wisdom. In Hebrew, chokmah: the gift Solomon asked for, a listening, understanding heart that can tell good from evil. Today's word.
Your line: an understanding heart. Today, before one decision, listen longer than feels efficient. Day four hundred seven.

fork.setup: you're Solomon. two women claim the same baby, there are no witnesses, and everyone is waiting for the king's judgment. what do you do?

fork.reveal: he calls for a sword. one woman agrees; the other begs him to give the child away alive. Solomon gives the baby to her: she is the mother.

original.note: Hebrew: wisdom, skill for living well. In Greek, sophia; in the Latin of the Church, sapientia.

trapdoor: what you thought: wisdom means being smart.
what it means: Solomon asks for a heart that listens and tells good from evil, and proves it by reading a mother's love.
what a scholar hears: lev shomea, a hearing heart. and the Book of Wisdom, in the Catholic canon, retells the request in Solomon's voice.

408.title: The Temple (1 Kings 8)
408.hook: the heaven of heavens can't contain God, yet he chooses to dwell
408.howItsDone: Catholic churches keep the Blessed Sacrament in a tabernacle, usually with a sanctuary lamp burning nearby, and Catholics genuflect toward it; the Church also keeps feasts for the dedication of churches, including the Lateran Basilica in Rome.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon was offered anything, and asked for wisdom. Your line was an understanding heart. Where did you listen before deciding? Day four hundred eight.

Seven years of building. Cedar from Lebanon, stone cut at the quarry so no hammer is heard on the site, gold over the inner walls. Solomon has built a house for God in Jerusalem, on the hill above his father's city. Now comes the day of dedication. The priests carry the ark of the covenant, the same ark David danced before, into the innermost room, the Holy of Holies, and set it under the wings of the cherubim. They step back out. And then something happens that nobody planned: a cloud fills the house. So thick that the priests can't stand to do their work. The text says the glory of the Lord had filled the house.
screen: `SEVEN YEARS OF BUILDING.` → `THE ARK INTO THE HOLY OF HOLIES.` → `A CLOUD FILLS THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Solomon stands before the altar in front of the whole assembly, spreads his hands toward heaven, and prays. And right in the middle of the proudest day of his reign, he says something that undercuts his own building. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is it then to be thought that God should indeed dwell upon earth? for if heaven, and the heavens of heavens cannot contain thee, how much less this house which I have built?" He knows. No building can hold God. The whole sky can't. So what is the Temple for? Solomon answers in the rest of the prayer: so that God's eyes may be open on this house night and day, and God will hear whoever prays toward it. The sick, the guilty, the soldier far away, even the foreigner who comes from a distant land. The Temple isn't a box for God. It's a place God chooses, freely, to be found. That's the line to hold: he can't be contained, and still he chooses to dwell. Catholics see that choice taken further. John's Gospel says the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and Jesus calls his own body a temple. Saint Paul tells Christians they themselves are God's temple. And in Catholic churches there's a tabernacle, often with a lamp burning beside it, where the Blessed Sacrament is kept, because Catholics believe Christ is truly present there. People kneel or genuflect as they pass. Solomon's question still stands: can God really dwell on earth? The Catholic answer is yes: not because anyone built something big enough, but because, Catholics say, he chooses to.
screen: `CAN GOD DWELL UPON EARTH?` · `A PLACE WHERE GOD WILL HEAR.` · `THE WORD DWELT AMONG US.` · `THE TABERNACLE AND ITS LAMP.` · then, large: `THE HEAVENS OF HEAVENS CANNOT CONTAIN THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make a small space holy. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are and pick one small spot: a corner of a shelf, a windowsill, the dashboard, a bedside table. Picture what could mark it as a place to stop. A candle, a cross, a picture of someone you love, a stone from a walk, an empty space kept clear on purpose. It doesn't need to be big. Solomon knew size wasn't the point. If you pray, you can ask God to meet you there. If you don't, let it be a place you come back to yourself. The bell holds the time.
The Temple. The house Solomon built in Jerusalem, filled with God's glory, which he knew could never contain God, a place God chose to be found. Today's word.
Your line: he chooses to dwell. Today, set aside your small space, and stop there once before the day is done. Day four hundred eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Temple was where God lived.
what it means: Solomon knew no house could hold God. the Temple was the place God chose to be found, and where prayers would be heard.
what a scholar hears: 2 Samuel 7 plays on bayit: David wants to build God a house, and God promises to build David a house, a dynasty, instead. Solomon's Temple sits where the two meet.

409.title: The widow's jar (1 Kings 17)
409.hook: a widow shares her last flour with Elijah and it doesn't run out
409.howItsDone: Catholics hear the widow of Zarephath at Mass, paired in one Sunday cycle with the poor widow who gave her two coins in the Gospel of Mark, and parishes often point to her when speaking of giving from need rather than surplus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Temple filled with a cloud, and Solomon admitted no house could hold God. Your line was he chooses to dwell. Did you find your small space? Day four hundred nine.

A prophet walks out of nowhere and tells a king to his face: no dew, no rain, until I say so. His name is Elijah, Elias in the Douay-Rheims, and the king is Ahab, who has turned Israel to the worship of Baal. Then the drought comes, and Elijah has to hide. God sends him to a brook, where ravens bring him bread and meat morning and evening. Then the brook dries up. And God sends him somewhere surprising: out of Israel, to Zarephath, a town of Sidon, the homeland of Ahab's queen, Jezebel. I have commanded a widow there to feed you, God says. Elijah arrives at the town gate, and there she is, picking up sticks.
screen: `NO DEW, NO RAIN.` → `RAVENS, THEN A DRY BROOK.` → `A WIDOW GATHERING STICKS.`

segments.voice: Elijah asks her for a little water. As she goes, he calls after her: and bring me a piece of bread. And she stops, and tells him the truth, in the Douay: "I have no bread, but only a handful of meal in a pot, and a little oil in a cruse." She's gathering two sticks to cook it for herself and her son, "that we may eat it, and die." That's where she is. One last meal, then nothing. And Elijah says the hardest, strangest thing: Fear not. Go and do it. But first make me a little cake, and bring it to me. Then make some for yourself and your son. Because the Lord says the pot of meal will not run out and the jar of oil will not fail until the day the rain comes. Think about what that asks. A foreign stranger wants the first bite of her last meal, on the strength of a promise from his God, not hers. And she does it. The text tells it simply: she went and did according to the word of Elias. And from that day, the meal wasted not, and the oil was not diminished. The text never says the pot filled. It says it never ran out. Just enough, day after day. Later in the chapter her son falls ill and stops breathing, and Elijah carries him upstairs, stretches himself over the boy three times, and cries to God, and the child lives. Centuries later, Jesus stands in the synagogue at Nazareth and reminds his hometown: there were many widows in Israel in Elijah's time, and he was sent to none of them, but to a widow of Sarepta in Sidon. The outsider who shared her last flour.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF MEAL, A LITTLE OIL.` · `FIRST MAKE ME A LITTLE CAKE.` · `ENOUGH, EVERY MORNING.` · `JESUS REMEMBERS HER AT NAZARETH.` · then, large: `THE POT OF MEAL WASTED NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share from what's scarce. Settle, and breathe. Think about what you have least of right now. Maybe it's money. Maybe time, or energy, or patience at the end of the day. Name it. Now think of one person who could use a little of exactly that. Not from your surplus. From the bottom of the pot. Picture giving them a small piece of it: ten minutes, a meal, a few dollars, a gentle answer when you're worn out. Notice the fear that comes up, and don't argue with it. If you pray, you can hand that fear to God. The bell holds the time.
Zarephath. The town where a starving widow fed a stranger first, and found the pot of meal and jar of oil never ran out. Today's word.
Your line: the jar did not fail. Today, give one small thing from what you have least of, and see what's left at the bottom tomorrow. Day four hundred nine.

410.title: Fire on Carmel (1 Kings 18)
410.hook: Elijah on Mount Carmel, where Carmelites later trace their roots
410.howItsDone: Carmelite friars, nuns and lay Carmelites honor Elijah as their spiritual father and keep his feast, and Catholics who wear the brown scapular do so in honor of Our Lady of Mount Carmel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow in Zarephath, a handful of flour, and a pot that never ran dry. Your line was the jar did not fail. What did you give from the bottom of the pot? Day four hundred ten.

The third year of the drought. The fields are dust. King Ahab calls Elijah the troubler of Israel, and Elijah answers: it's you who troubled Israel, by following Baal. Then he makes a proposal. Gather everyone on Mount Carmel, the ridge above the sea. Bring the prophets of Baal, four hundred and fifty of them. And there, in front of the whole nation, we'll settle it. Two altars, two bulls, no fire. Each side calls on its God. The God who answers by fire, he is God. And the people, the Douay-Rheims says, answered: "A very good proposal."
screen: `THE THIRD YEAR OF DROUGHT.` → `EVERYONE TO MOUNT CARMEL.` → `THE GOD WHO ANSWERS BY FIRE.`

segments.voice: Before any fire, Elijah turns to the crowd, and that's where today's line comes from. In the Douay: "How long do you halt between two sides? if the Lord be God, follow him." To halt is to limp. Some readers hear in the Hebrew someone hobbling back and forth between two paths, never putting full weight on either. The people had not quite rejected the God of Israel. They just kept Baal on the side, in case. And the text says they answered him not a word. Then the contest. The prophets of Baal call from morning till noon, and there is no voice, no answer. Elijah rebuilds the Lord's broken-down altar with twelve stones, one for each tribe, and has it soaked with water, three times, until the trench overflows. Then he prays, simply: let this people know that thou art the Lord God, and that thou hast turned their heart again. And the fire of the Lord falls, and burns up the offering, the wood, the stones, even the water in the trench. The people fall on their faces: the Lord he is God. Then Elijah climbs to the top of Carmel, puts his face between his knees, and sends his servant to look at the sea seven times. On the seventh: a little cloud, like a man's foot. Then the rain. Here's the Catholic thread. Centuries later, hermits settled on Mount Carmel, tradition says near a spring named for Elijah. They became the Carmelites, the order of Saint Teresa of Avila, Saint John of the Cross and Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, and they honor Elijah as their spiritual father. Carmelite tradition even saw in that little rising cloud a figure of Mary.
screen: `HOW LONG WILL YOU LIMP?` · `NO VOICE FROM MORNING TILL NOON.` · `FIRE ON A SOAKED ALTAR.` · `HERMITS ON CARMEL: THE CARMELITES.` · then, large: `THE LORD HE IS GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray on a hill or high place. If you can, go somewhere higher than usual: a hill, a top-floor window, a staircase landing, even a step. If you can't, picture Carmel: the ridge, the sea below. Settle, and breathe. Then ask yourself Elijah's question: where am I limping between two sides? Something you half believe, half hedge on. Don't answer it out loud yet. Just notice where your weight is. If you pray, you can do as Elijah did, face down or head bowed, and wait. The bell holds the time.
Carmel. The mountain where Elijah's contest proved the Lord answers by fire, and where the Carmelites later found their roots. Today's word.
Your line: how long will you halt. Today, pick one thing you've been undecided about for too long, and put your full weight down on one side. Day four hundred ten.

411.title: The still small voice (1 Kings 19)
411.hook: not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but a gentle whisper; the Douay says a whistling of a gentle air
411.carry: a whistling of a gentle air
411.howItsDone: Catholics hear Elijah under the broom tree at Sunday Mass alongside Jesus's teaching on the bread of life, and many seek God's quiet voice in silent prayer, retreats and Eucharistic adoration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fire on Carmel, and a prophet asking a hedging people to choose. Your line was how long will you halt. Where did you put your weight down? Day four hundred eleven.

The day after fire falls from heaven should be the best day of Elijah's life. It isn't. Queen Jezebel sends him a message: by this time tomorrow, you're dead. And the bold prophet of Carmel runs. A day's walk into the desert, alone. He sits under a broom tree, the Douay-Rheims calls it a juniper, and asks to die: "It is enough for me, Lord, take away my soul." Then he falls asleep. Despair, the day after a great victory. And God's first answer isn't a lecture. An angel touches him and says: arise and eat. There's bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water by his head.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER THE FIRE.` → `UNDER THE JUNIPER: IT IS ENOUGH.` → `ARISE AND EAT.`

segments.voice: He eats, sleeps, and the angel comes again: "Arise, eat: for thou hast yet a great way to go." And in the strength of that food he walks forty days and nights to Horeb, the mountain of God, where Moses once saw the burning bush. He crawls into a cave. And God asks him a question: What dost thou here, Elias? Elijah pours out his complaint: I've been zealous, they've killed the prophets, and I alone am left. God says: go out, and stand on the mountain, for the Lord is passing by. Then a great wind tears at the mountains and breaks the rocks. The Lord is not in the wind. Then an earthquake. Not in the earthquake. Then fire, the very thing God answered with on Carmel. Not in the fire. And after the fire, the King James says, "a still small voice." The Douay, following the Latin, gives it as "a whistling of a gentle air." The Hebrew is even stranger: a voice of thin silence. Translators have rendered it many ways, because it describes something almost not there. And when Elijah hears it, he covers his face with his cloak and steps out. Notice: God doesn't fix Elijah's mood. He asks the same question again, and then gives him work: go back, anoint a new king, anoint Elisha. And a correction: you're not alone; seven thousand in Israel haven't bowed to Baal. The Church hears two things here. The bread that carried Elijah forty days is read alongside Jesus's words about the bread of life. And Catholic contemplatives often point to the whisper when they speak of silence: God, they say, can be found in the quietest sound.
screen: `FOOD FOR A GREAT WAY TO GO.` · `WHAT DOST THOU HERE, ELIAS?` · `NOT THE WIND, QUAKE, OR FIRE.` · `A VOICE OF THIN SILENCE.` · then, large: `A WHISTLING OF A GENTLE AIR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen for the quietest sound. Settle, and breathe. First notice the loud things: traffic, a fridge hum, voices, your own thoughts. Let them pass, like the wind and the earthquake. Then listen underneath them, for the smallest sound you can find. A breath. A ticking. Something almost nothing. Stay with it. If you pray, you can listen for God there, with no words of your own. And if you've been running on empty like Elijah, notice that too. The story's first answer was bread and sleep. The bell holds the time.
Horeb. The mountain of God where Elijah heard, not in wind, quake or fire, but in a whisper the Douay calls a whistling of a gentle air. Today's word.
Your line: a whistling of a gentle air. Today, turn off one source of noise for ten minutes, and listen to what's left. Day four hundred eleven.

what it means: a burned-out prophet is fed, given rest, and met not in power but in near-silence, and then sent back with work and company.
what a scholar hears: qol demamah daqqah, a voice of thin silence, a phrase translators have rendered many ways because it describes almost nothing at all.

412.title: The chariot of fire (2 Kings 2)
412.hook: Elisha asks a double portion of Elijah's spirit, and the mantle falls
412.howItsDone: Catholics hear Elijah's taking up and Elisha's call in the weekday Mass readings, and remember both on their feast days in the Carmelite calendar; Elijah appears again in the Gospel of the Transfiguration, read each Lent and on August 6.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elijah at Horeb, hearing God not in the wind or the fire, but in a whisper. Your line was a whistling of a gentle air. What did you hear in the quiet? Day four hundred twelve.

Everybody seems to know what's going to happen today except the person it's happening to, and he knows too. Elijah is walking his last road, and his young disciple Elisha, Eliseus in the Douay-Rheims, is walking beside him. At each town, Elijah says: stay here, the Lord has sent me on ahead. And three times Elisha answers: "As the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee." At Bethel and again at Jericho, the sons of the prophets come out and ask Elisha: you know the Lord is taking your master today? And he says: I know. Hold your peace. They reach the Jordan.
screen: `ELIJAH'S LAST ROAD.` → `I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE.` → `I KNOW. HOLD YOUR PEACE.`

segments.voice: At the river, Elijah rolls up his mantle, the rough cloak that marked him as a prophet, and strikes the water. It parts, and the two cross on dry ground, the way Israel once crossed. Then Elijah asks: what shall I do for thee, before I be taken away? And Elisha asks big. The Douay says "thy double spirit"; many English Bibles say a double portion. In Israel, a firstborn son inherited a double share. Elisha is asking to be Elijah's heir, his son in the spirit. Elijah says: thou hast asked a hard thing. If you see me when I'm taken, it's yours. They keep walking and talking. And suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire comes between them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. Notice the detail: the chariot separates them; the whirlwind carries him up. Elisha sees it, and cries out: "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the driver thereof." He tears his clothes in grief. Then he looks down. Elijah's mantle has fallen. He picks it up, walks back to the Jordan, and strikes the water with it, asking, where is the God of Elijah? And the water parts. The prophets watching from across the river say: the spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha. This is a scene about handing on. A teacher doesn't live forever, but what God gave through him can pass to another, the way a cloak falls into new hands. And Elijah's story isn't finished: centuries later he appears with Moses beside Jesus on the mountain of the Transfiguration.
screen: `THE MANTLE PARTS THE JORDAN.` · `ASKING FOR A DOUBLE PORTION.` · `CHARIOT BETWEEN, WHIRLWIND UP.` · `THE MANTLE FALLS TO ELISHA.` · then, large: `MY FATHER, MY FATHER, THE CHARIOT OF ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a teacher's mantle. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who taught you something that lasted. A grandparent who showed you how to pray. A coach, a teacher, a priest or sister, a mentor at work, a friend who walked you through a hard year. Maybe they're gone now. Picture what they left behind for you: a habit, a phrase, a way of treating people. That's their mantle. Imagine bending down and picking it up. If you pray, you can ask that some of what was in them carry on in you. The bell holds the time.
Elisha. The disciple who watched Elijah taken up by a whirlwind, and picked up the mantle that fell to him. Today's word.
Your line: pick up the mantle. Today, do one thing the way someone who taught you would have done it, on purpose, in their honor. Day four hundred twelve.

413.title: Naaman (2 Kings 5)
413.hook: a proud general is told to wash seven times in a muddy river
413.howItsDone: Catholics hear Naaman's healing at Mass in Lent, alongside Jesus recalling him at Nazareth, and the Church has long read his washing in the Jordan as a figure of baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chariot of fire, and Elisha picking up Elijah's fallen mantle. Your line was pick up the mantle. Whose way of doing things did you honor? Day four hundred thirteen, the end of week fifty-nine.

The person who sets this story moving doesn't even get a name. She's a little girl from Israel, carried off by raiders from Syria, now a servant to the wife of the Syrian army's commander. That commander is Naaman: a great man, honored, brave, rich, and a leper. And one day this captive girl, a servant in a stranger's house, says to her mistress: I wish my master were with the prophet in Samaria. He would heal him. That's all. One sentence of kindness from a kidnapped child, and a general packs up silver, gold, ten changes of clothes, and a letter from his king.
screen: `A CAPTIVE GIRL FROM ISRAEL.` → `A GREAT GENERAL, AND A LEPER.` → `ONE SENTENCE OF KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Naaman arrives at Elisha's door with his horses and chariots, the full parade. And Elisha doesn't even come out. He sends a messenger with a short instruction, in the Douay-Rheims: "Go, and wash seven times in the Jordan." Naaman is furious. He'd pictured the prophet coming out, calling on his God, waving a hand over the spot, something worthy of a general. And the Jordan? Aren't the rivers of Damascus better than all the waters of Israel? He turns to leave in a rage. Then his servants, gently, say the line that turns the whole story: "if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, surely thou shouldst have done it: how much rather what he now hath said to thee: Wash, and thou shalt be clean?" If he'd asked for something heroic, you'd have done it. He asked for something simple. So Naaman goes down to the river and dips himself seven times. And his flesh, the Douay says, became "like the flesh of a little child." Like the girl who started all this. He goes back and says: now I know there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. Elisha refuses any payment at all. Notice who carried the healing to Naaman: a captive girl, a messenger, his own servants. Jesus remembers him in the synagogue at Nazareth: many lepers in Israel in Elisha's time, and none was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian. Catholic tradition sees baptism here: going down into the water, coming up like a newborn. The Church reads this story in Lent, as people prepare for baptism at Easter.
screen: `THE PROPHET DOESN'T COME OUT.` · `GO, AND WASH SEVEN TIMES.` · `IF HE'D ASKED A GREAT THING.` · `FLESH LIKE A LITTLE CHILD'S.` · then, large: `WASH, AND THOU SHALT BE CLEAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do the humble simple thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of a problem where the answer is probably obvious and small, and you've been waiting for something bigger. The apology you could just say. The doctor you could just call. The walk, the glass of water, the early night. If a voice says that's too simple to matter, that's Naaman at the riverbank. If you pray, you can ask for the humility to go down to the water. Then picture yourself doing the simple thing, once. The bell holds the time.
Naaman. The proud Syrian general healed of leprosy when he finally did the simple thing and washed seven times in the Jordan. Today's word.

Your line: go and wash. Today, do the small humble thing you've been avoiding. And that's week fifty-nine: wisdom, the Temple, the widow's jar, Carmel, the whisper, the mantle, and Naaman. Day four hundred thirteen.
